title: Sacrifices Fest
summary: Keep offering the queen with check until the king and rook can be attacked together; compare why an early change of checking file can lose the win.

nodes.question: Can the queen keep checking while apparently hanging?
nodes.explanation: Begin after ...Kxg3. White has Ka3, Qh1, b7 and d5 against Kg3 and rooks on b2/b1. The last white kingside pawn has just disappeared.

branches.title: Finish the checking sequence and promote
commentary: Begin after ...Kxg3. White has Ka3, Qh1, b7 and d5 against Kg3 and rooks on b2/b1. The last white kingside pawn has just disappeared.
Qg1+ keeps the king moving while the queen remains available to the rook on b1. The rook’s first priority is still stopping b8.
Kf3 declines the queen offer and steps toward the center.
Qf1+ changes the checking line and again offers the queen to the rook.
Ke3 continues the source king walk.
Qc1+ forks Ke3 and Rb1, while offering the queen for the sixth time across the source’s larger sequence. Only the final three offers are encoded here.
Rxc1 captures the queen, leaving the rook on b2 available for the white king to capture.
Kxb2 removes that rook and guards b1. The remaining rook cannot return through b1 to blockade b8.
Rc2+ tries to keep checking along the second rank.
Kb1 answers the check while controlling b2, preventing a rook transfer through that square.
Rc4 is the final illustrated rook placement. It does not stop the b7 pawn from promoting.
b8=Q is an independently completed promotion after the last saved diagram. The exact queen-and-pawn versus rook ending is winning for White.

branches.title: Independent capture of the first offered queen
commentary: This independently selected legal comparison tests the rook capture in the supported later diagram, rather than assuming the earlier larger variation is identical.
Qg1+ gives check and leaves the queen on the rook’s rank.
Rxg1 accepts the queen but abandons the defense of Rb2.
Kxb2 removes the second rook and protects the b1 entry square. White retains a checked win.
Rg2+ tries a horizontal check, using the remaining rook.
Kb1 meets the check and protects b2. The exact position is winning for White; further conversion is outside this branch.

branches.explanation: Kb1 meets the check and protects b2. The exact position is winning for White; further conversion is outside this branch.

branches.title: An early f-file switch allows a draw
commentary: This independently tested comparison changes the king retreat from f3 to f4. White cannot assume the same immediate queen move will still preserve the win.
Qg1+ begins correctly, keeping the forcing checks available.
Kf4 selects another legal flight. White still has a forced win, but must choose the next queen maneuver carefully.
Qf1+ checks but prematurely switches to the f-file. Unlike the source continuation with the king on f3, this exact position is drawn with best play.
Ke5 preserves the draw in this independent representative defense. Black declines the queen offer and avoids the source’s e3 square, where Qc1+ would enable the winning exchange.

exercises.prompt: Why does capturing the queen fail to solve Black’s problem?
exercises.answer: The white king can capture Rb2 and guard b1. That denies the remaining rook its direct route behind the promotion square while b7 remains ready to advance.

startContext: Begin after ...Kxg3 at 148 seconds, the visually reconstructed seven-piece position. Earlier ten/eight-piece queen and rook maneuvers remain source context. The final three illustrated queen offers are checked, with b8=Q explicitly supplied after the final source diagram; two additional comparisons use independent representative replies, including a drawing error after a different king retreat.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
